pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Read and write Roman numerals to 100 (I, V, X, L, C and combinations, incl. subtractive pairs like IV, IX, XL) and convert to/from Hindu-Arabic. The deeper aim: appreciate BY CONTRAST that our system has place value and a zero, which Roman numerals lack — illuminating why place value is powerful.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): not a CCSS-M topic; taught in some US curricula as enrichment/history of number.
• Operational details — Teach the symbol values and the additive rule (XVII = 10+5+1+1), then the subtractive rule (IV = 5−1, IX, XL, XC) as the tricky exception. Convert both directions. Crucially, run the CONTRAST explicitly: try 'writing' large or zero quantities in Roman and feel the absence of place value and a placeholder — making our base-ten system's efficiency vivid.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): reads/writes additive numerals (XVII, LX). Tier B (age 8-9, secure): handles subtractive pairs (XLIV = 44) both directions. Tier C (age 9, extending): explains why Roman has no zero/place value and why that makes calculation harder.
bestPractices: Teach symbol values, then the additive rule, then subtractive pairs (IV, IX, XL, XC) as the key exception.
Practise conversion in both directions with real artefacts (clocks, dates, chapter numbers).
Run the explicit contrast: attempt a large number or 'zero' in Roman to FEEL the missing place value and placeholder.
Use the contrast to deepen appreciation of base-ten (position carries value; zero holds a place).
Watch the subtractive-notation errors (IIII vs IV, or invalid forms like IL).
keyRepresentations: Real artefacts: clock faces, monument dates, book chapters
Place-value chart as the contrast (what Roman lacks)
commonMisconceptions: Pure additive thinking, writing 4 as IIII or 9 as VIIII instead of IV/IX.
Inventing invalid subtractive forms (IL for 49 instead of XLIX).
Misordering symbols or ignoring the subtractive-position rule.
Thinking Roman numerals have a zero or place value.
Reading a subtractive pair additively (IX as 11).

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: read and write Roman numerals to 100 (I, V, X, L, C and their combinations, including subtractive pairs like IV, IX, XL, XC) and convert both ways to Hindu-Arabic numbers. The deeper aim is to appreciate BY CONTRAST that our base-ten system carries value by position and uses zero as a placeholder, which Roman numerals lack — making vivid why place value is powerful. Teach symbol values, then the additive rule (XVII = 10+5+1+1), then the subtractive rule (IV = 5-1) as the tricky exception, and run the contrast explicitly by trying to write numbers that need many repeated symbols, a very large number, and zero in Roman.

activities.title: Build-a-numeral bench with a contrast challenge
feedback: If IIII or VIIII is built, show the standard subtractive fix (IV = 5-1, IX = 10-1) and explain that a smaller symbol placed before a larger one in one of the allowed pairs (IV, IX, XL, XC) means subtract.
If an invalid form like IL is built for 49, show the valid XLIX and explain which subtractive pairs are allowed (IV, IX, XL, XC).

During the contrast challenge, place the Roman form beside the tidy base-ten numeral and name the real limits: unwieldy strings of repeated symbols (long for 88, far longer for a number like 3,000 within the taught set, with conventional large-number symbols like M lying beyond the taught set), and genuinely no symbol at all to put where our zero sits.
activities.rationale: Building and converting numerals by action with immediate correction surfaces the subtractive exception at the moment of error, and staging the 'write a long numeral / write zero' challenge lets the learner feel the absence of place value and a placeholder rather than just be told about it. A live value display and invalid-form flagging make the additive-versus-subtractive mechanism concrete; these are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required technology.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
Contrasting Roman numerals with base-ten deepens appreciation of place value and the placeholder role of zero.
learnerActions: Place or drag symbol tiles (I, V, X, L, C) into a row and read the value aloud as you build, e.g. XVII = 10+5+1+1 = 17.
When you write 4 as IIII or 9 as VIIII, notice it is flagged and rewrite it the valid subtractive way (IV = 5-1, IX = 10-1).
Convert both directions: given 44, build XLIV; given XLIV, read it as 40 + 4.

Take the contrast challenge: write 88 (LXXXVIII) and notice how many repeated symbols it needs; then try a very large number like 3,000 and see how unwieldy it becomes — within the taught symbols you would need a huge string of C's, and the usual Roman form MMM uses M, a symbol beyond those you are taught; then try to write zero and find there is NO symbol at all — each shown beside the compact base-ten numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: Roman numerals combine fixed symbol values by adding (and sometimes subtracting the smaller-before-larger pair); because they have no place value and no zero placeholder, numbers with many repeats become unwieldy, very large numbers become enormous strings or need symbols beyond the basic set, and zero cannot be written at all — which is exactly why position-carries-value and a placeholder zero are powerful inventions.

activities.title: Talk to a Roman accountant about why the system changed
feedback: If the learner thinks the Roman system just needs a zero symbol added, point out that position must also carry value for zero to do its placeholder job.
Prompt the learner to connect the accountant's difficulty adding large numbers to the missing place value, not just unfamiliar symbols.
activities.rationale: A responsive dialogue may suit the history-of-number objective because the 'why did the system change?' story invites questioning and discussion; recognition tasks alone do not require the learner to articulate the reason. This is a proposed affordance rather than established superiority over other media, and it complements the building activity by foregrounding the reason behind the contrast.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
Contrasting Roman numerals with base-ten deepens appreciation of place value and the placeholder role of zero.
learnerActions: In role, interview a Roman merchant or scholar about how they wrote numbers and did sums.
Ask them to add two large numbers using only Roman numerals and notice where it gets hard.
Probe: why was there no way to write zero, and why did the world later adopt place value and zero?
Summarise in your own words what base-ten gives us that Roman numerals do not.
activities.intendedInsight: The history-of-number aim — that the numeral system changed over time to include zero and place value — can become meaningful through an unscripted 'why is this so hard?' exchange that carries the contrast the curriculum emphasises.

activities.title: Consolidate conversion with real artefacts and validity checks
feedback: If XLIV is read additively as 66, show that a smaller symbol before a larger one in an allowed pair (IV, IX, XL, XC) means subtract: XL = 50-10 = 40, IV = 5-1 = 4, so XLIV = 44.

If the learner says the first symbol 'is in the tens place', contrast directly: in 44 position sets value, but in XLIV each symbol keeps its own value and we add or subtract — Roman has no place value and no zero.
Reinforce the standard subtractive forms (IV, IX, XL, XC), reject invalid ones like IL, and treat IIII as a non-standard clock-face variant rather than the standard way to write 4.
activities.rationale: Conversion in both directions, validity-of-form checks and real artefacts anchor the skill in genuine contexts. Recognition and matching tasks are useful for consolidation and checking but do not by themselves require the learner to construct a full explanation, so pair them with the spoken 'how do the two 4s differ?' prompt.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
learnerActions: Read Roman numerals on real artefacts — clock faces, monument or building dates, book chapter numbers — and write their Hindu-Arabic values (note that many clocks show 4 as IIII, a traditional variant; the standard written form is IV).
Write given numbers (e.g. 44, 49, 88) in Roman numerals, choosing valid subtractive forms.
Decide which of several forms is valid for a number like 49 (XLIX, not IL) and explain why.
Explain aloud how the two 4s in 44 differ (40 and 4 by position) and why XLIV instead uses subtraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent two-way conversion and recognising valid versus invalid forms consolidate the reading/writing skill, while explaining the two 4s in 44 reinforces the place-value contrast.

activities.title: Reference chart and annotated clock face
feedback: When a learner uncovers a numeral's make-up, confirm whether it is additive (VII = 5+1+1) or subtractive (IX = 10-1).
Use the adjacent place-value chart to point out there is no column or symbol in Roman that behaves like our zero placeholder.
activities.rationale: A fixed chart or annotated image is a valuable reference and can teach symbol values, though it cannot itself be manipulated to compute values or stage the contrast — so it supports rather than replaces the building and dialogue activities.
learnerActions: Keep a symbol-to-value reference to hand (I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100).
Tap or point to each clock numeral to reveal its value and whether it is built additively or subtractively.
Use a side-by-side Roman | Hindu-Arabic chart to check your conversions, and a place-value chart alongside to see what Roman lacks.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference supports recall of symbol values and makes the additive/subtractive make-up of familiar numerals (like clock numbers) explicit.

constraints: The deeper objective is conceptual appreciation of place value and zero by contrast, not just symbol decoding; the contrast must be run explicitly (try to write a long numeral, a very large number, and zero in Roman).

Recognition and matching tasks consolidate and check the skill but do not by themselves elicit an independent spoken or written explanation of why our system differs; include a construct-an-explanation prompt.
A static chart or annotated image teaches symbol values and make-up but cannot be manipulated to compute values live or stage the balloon/zero contrast; treat it as a reference scaffold.

Valid subtractive forms are IV, IX, XL, XC; when writing, treat IIII and VIIII as non-standard (use IV and IX), noting that IIII is a traditional variant still seen on many clock faces, and reject invalid forms such as IL (for 49, use XLIX).
Roman numerals genuinely have no zero symbol and no positional place value — present this as the real system contrast, not as a claim about any particular teaching medium being uniquely necessary.

This topic teaches symbols I to C only; large numbers (e.g. 3,000) should be used to show how numerals become unwieldy within the taught set and that conventional large-number symbols such as M lie beyond those taught — not presented as part of the required symbol set, and not framed as literally 'running out' of symbols.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the arithmetic and logic: XVII = 10+5+1+1 = 17 (correct); XL = 50-10 = 40 and IV = 5-1 = 4, so XLIV = 44 (correct); LXXXVIII = 88 (correct); XLIX = 49 is the valid form, IL is invalid. The legacy additive misreading 'XLIV = 66' is retained only as an error pattern to correct, never as a valid answer.

The row's contrast example '3,000' is conventionally MMM (uses M, outside the taught I–C range); within the taught set it would require roughly thirty C's, i.e. an unwieldy ballooning string. It is therefore treated as a ballooning/beyond-taught illustration, NOT as a case of 'running out of symbols'. The only genuine 'no symbol at all' case is zero.

Two cited sources (CCSS-M absence note and NCETM place-value PD) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Evidence strength is not upgraded here.
Comparative-efficacy wording about dialogue versus recognition has been softened to proposed/may phrasing; the source row does not establish superiority of any medium.

probeDeeper: In 44, how is the first 4 different from the second 4?
Does the Roman system have a symbol for zero? Why does our system need one?
Read XLIV and split it into its chunks.
assess.correctAnswer: XLIV = 44 (XL = 40 by subtraction, IV = 4 by subtraction). It differs because Roman numerals combine symbols by value with no place value and no zero, whereas in 44 the two 4s mean different amounts (40 and 4) because of their POSITION, and we use 0 to hold empty places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads Roman numerals additively, ignoring subtractive order: XLIV = 10 + 50 + 1 + 5 = 66
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show smaller-before-larger means subtract: XL = 50 − 10 = 40, IV = 5 − 1 = 4. Re-read XLIV as 40 + 4.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child sums all symbols regardless of a smaller-before-larger pair.

errorPatterns.pattern: Imports place value into Roman numerals — thinks a symbol's position gives it a tens/ones value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast directly: in 44 position sets value; in XLIV each symbol keeps its own value and we add/subtract. Roman has no zero and no place value.
errorPatterns.distractor: In XLIV the symbols get tens/ones values from their position, just like 44.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the first symbol 'is in the tens place' or that our 44 and XLIV work the same way.

responseLevels.gap: Reads Roman numerals additively (XLIV = 66) or claims they work like place value.
responseLevels.full: Reads/writes Roman numerals to 100 with subtraction and explains that Roman lacks place value and zero, unlike our positional system.
responseLevels.partial: Converts simple Roman numerals but cannot articulate why our place-value system (with zero) differs.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask: 'Read XLIV for me. Now tell me: how is the Roman way of writing forty-four different from the way we write 44? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Contrasting XLIV with 44 forces the child to articulate what place value actually does. A child who understands names position (the two 4s differ) and the role of zero; a child who doesn't either reads Roman additively (66) or wrongly imports place value into the Roman symbols. The reason tier exposes the systems contrast.
